3.0.s.en: (1) The person of John the Baptist

3.0.0.en: "In those days": that is, when Christ drew near to the age of thirty, and precisely six months before it, John the Baptist appeared, who was six months older than He.

3.0.1.en: "John the Baptist": he is John the son of Zacharias the priest, who became famous for baptizing the Jews, and so was called the Baptist, and who lived about thirty years in the wilderness in a life of asceticism, as a model of monasticism in the Old Testament and of the love of prayer and solitude. This was a spiritual period in which he was prepared for the greatest service, which was preparing the way for the proclamation of Christ and His redemption.

3.0.2.en: "Preaching": he began his preaching after thirty years of silence, and called the people to repentance and to return to God. "The wilderness of Judaea": it lies east of Jerusalem, near the Dead Sea (the Sea of Lot).

3.1.0.en: His preaching was of repentance, that is, the purification of the heart from sin, and a change of direction from evil to life with God.

3.1.1.en: "At hand": because after six months the preaching of Christ would begin, who reigns over hearts with a heavenly kingship. His warning was clear, namely the nearness of the Kingdom of Heaven, that is, the reign of Christ over hearts, which is a heavenly, spiritual reign, and not an earthly one as the Jews imagined, to rescue them from the cruelty of the Romans. He preached the Kingdom of God over the heart, so that a person may be made fit to dwell in heaven and reign with God forever; and God cannot reign over a heart that clings to sin and refuses repentance.

3.2.0.en: In this verse Matthew the Evangelist, who addresses the Jews, cites the prophecy of Isaiah, who was famous and well known among the Jews, to confirm the preparing of the way of the expected Messiah (Isa 40:3). It is said of John that he is a "voice", to distinguish him from Christ, who is the Word Himself. And in his preaching he was strong, like one who cries out and proclaims the preparing of the way of God in the heart, that is, by repentance and the good conduct that results from it.

3.2.1.en: "Prepare ye the way of the Lord": to remove the obstacles, as the herald used to cry out to prepare for the passing of a king or a great man; what is meant here is the removal of sins and pride from the heart.

3.2.2.en: "Make his paths straight": by keeping away from hypocrisy and evil, that is, correcting what is crooked, so that the heart is upright and God may pass through it and fill it with ease.

3.3.0.en: He describes the ascetic life that John the Baptist lived: his clothing was of coarse camel's hair, and not soft garments. As for the girdle that he wore about his loins, that is, his waist and belly, it was of leather, and not an expensive, decorated one.

3.3.1.en: As for his food, it was locusts, the well-known insect, though there is another opinion that it was a wild plant, in addition to wild honey which bees make in the clefts of the rocks.

3.3.2.en: The meaning of this is that he was content with necessary clothing and food, because his heart was occupied with heavenly things and the service of God. He is an image of the monastic life in the Old Testament, like Elijah the prophet.

3.4.0.en: In view of the depth and spirituality of John's preaching and its strong effect on hearts, most of the inhabitants of Jerusalem went out to him, and indeed all the region of Judea and all the lands surrounding the river Jordan; and he said "all" as an indication of the majority.

3.5.0.en: And being moved by his sermons, they came forward to be baptized, each one of them, in the river Jordan, confessing his sins. This was a baptism of repentance, and a clear indication of the sacrament of confession at the hand of the priest in the New Testament. Baptism was known among the Jews, for they used to baptize proselyte Gentiles when they joined them. So baptism was familiar to them, but the addition here is repentance and confession. As for the baptism of the New Testament, it differs from the baptism of John in that it is by the Holy Spirit, to change human nature, so that it becomes pure from every sin.

3.5.1.en: It is clear that the baptism of repentance is a preparation for the baptism of the New Testament. And this is what takes place now, when a person confesses his sins, if he is an adult, before receiving the sacrament of Baptism.

3.5.2.en: Repentance is your way of preparing your heart so that Christ may dwell in it. So do not neglect the voices of God crying out to you for repentance through the Holy Bible and the teachings of the Church, and also through those around you and their rebuke of you, but hasten to repent before God every day, and then at the hand of the priest, to receive forgiveness of your sins.

3.6.0.en: The Pharisees: a party that appeared in the second century BC in Jewish society, holding to the Law literally, and they were regarded as the leaders of Jewish thought; the meaning of their name is "the separated", that is, those chosen by God. They trusted in their righteousness, and said: if two enter heaven, at least one of them is a Pharisee. The Sadducees: a party that objected to the authority of the Pharisees and denied eternal life and spirits. They shared with the Pharisees in the spiritual leadership of the Jews, and were regarded as the rich aristocratic class, and they were descendants of Zadok the priest.

3.6.1.en: They came to John not for repentance, but to get to know John, who had drawn the crowds away from them. Perhaps they were seeking a position of leadership behind this new leader to whom all the Jews had gone out. John the Baptist was strong, and confronted them with the crookedness of their hearts, since in appearance they sought repentance while inwardly they were far from it, so he rebuked them, describing them as a "generation of vipers", a kind of snake marked by great cunning and craftiness, and whose young eat their mother's belly and kill her in order to come out to life; that is, he described them as selfish and hard-hearted.

3.6.2.en: "The wrath to come": that is, the judgment of God on the last day, before which they must stand, and he marveled at their neglect of repentance and of preparation for eternity, though they were the teachers of the Jews, by his saying: "who hath warned you".

3.7.0.en: John calls them to prove their repentance by doing the works of repentance, that is, forsaking sin and doing what is good; for without fruit, however much they speak about repentance, it profits them nothing, and likewise their baptism would be of no benefit to them.

3.8.0.en: He also rebukes them for their pride, since they supposed that by their claim to descent from Abraham, the man of the promises, they would receive the promises. But God requires the one who walks in the righteousness of Abraham, to be a true son of his. "These stones": he points to stones that were before him. Just as God created Adam from dust, He is also able to create children for Abraham from stones.

3.8.1.en: He also means that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from the stones, that is, the stony, hard hearts of the Gentiles who worship idols of stone, who, if they believe and walk in righteousness, become true children of Abraham.

3.8.2.en: Do not rely on being a Christian, but repent and do good, so that you may enjoy God's care and the Kingdom of Heaven. The name condemns you if you do not live by it, and likewise the honor of your family and your kinship to spiritual people does not benefit you, but calls you to imitate them, so that you live a life of repentance and do good like your Christ.

3.9.0.en: This "axe" is the wooden Cross, or the word of God, which condemns everyone who does not believe, and cuts him off from his root and destroys him, because he did not believe in Christ the Savior.

3.9.1.en: And the laying of the axe means the nearness of judgment, so repentance is necessary and presenting its proof, which is the fruits of righteousness; and if a person does not bring forth fruit, he should expect nothing but the eternal fire.

3.10.0.en: John distinguishes between the baptism of repentance and the baptism of Christ, God the Word, which is by the Holy Spirit, to renew human nature; and although he is the leader of the baptism of repentance, yet in relation to Christ he is not worthy to be the least slave in His service, to whom the carrying of the sandals is entrusted.

3.10.1.en: The humility of the Baptist appears from this, for although he was the strongest of the prophets, he denied himself, giving glory to Christ.

3.10.2.en: "The Holy Ghost and with fire": he means the baptism of the Holy Spirit which renews nature, and the fire burns up evil and the nature inclined to sin, to renew a person for life with God.

3.11.0.en: In the end John the Baptist proclaims Christ the Judge, and likens Him to the farmer who separates the grain from the chaff after the process of threshing, using for this the winnowing fork, that is, the pitchfork, which is a shaft with wooden fingers by which the grain mixed with straw is lifted, so the grain falls quickly, while the chaff or straw flies off and falls far away. In this way the grain is gathered by itself, and the straw by itself, and this is done in a wide place beside the field called the threshing floor. Then the grain is gathered into sacks and put in the granary, while the straw is burned with fire since it is not needed.

3.11.1.en: The winnowing fork: it is the word of God, or the Cross, by which God judges the unbelievers and the unrepentant. The threshing floor: it is the end of the world, and the day of judgment.

3.11.2.en: The granary: it is the Kingdom of Heaven or the Church.

3.11.3.en: The fire: it is the eternal torment.

3.11.4.en: The chaff: they are the wicked.

3.11.5.en: The wheat: they are the believers who will be glorified with Christ in the heavens, and he says of them "his wheat", that is, those joined to Him who remain with Him in the Kingdom, unlike the chaff, that is, the wicked, of whom he does not say "his chaff" because they have separated from Him.

3.12.0.en: Christ lived His childhood and youth until the age of thirty in Nazareth and the region of Galilee, then turned south to Judea at the river Jordan, where the crowds had gathered around John the Baptist. And He came forward as a representative of mankind to be baptized with the baptism of repentance, though He is without sin, but bearing our sins, offering repentance on our behalf. "Then": he means the period in which John the Baptist was preaching, which was six months.

3.12.1.en: "Cometh": that is, He appeared openly among the crowds to share with us and to fulfill all righteousness on our behalf, though He has no need of repentance. "Jordan": he means the river Jordan, which extends about two hundred miles from the north of Israel to its south.

3.13.0.en: John knew by the Spirit that this was the expected Messiah, and he marveled at the humility of Christ, so he said to Him humbly that it was he who needed to be baptized by Him, so how could he baptize Him? And Christ replies with gentleness and greater humility, asking John to permit it and baptize Him, to fulfill all righteousness on behalf of sinful human beings, who were unable to fulfill it because they kept away from repentance and the righteous life.

3.13.1.en: Contemplate this wonderful love, so that you too may be humble, not only before those greater than you, but before those lower than you in position or age, and ask yourself: do I speak with gentleness and humility to every person?

3.14.0.en: Jesus went down into the river Jordan and was immersed in the water, then went up and came out of the water. For this reason the Church holds to the rite of immersion in the water of Baptism, because it means burial with Christ, then resurrection also with Him, as the Holy Bible says: "Buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him" (Col 2:12). And for the first time God manifests His three hypostases in full clarity: Christ the Son in the water, the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove upon His head, and the Father, whose voice they heard from heaven.

3.14.1.en: This was clear before John, who baptized Christ, and all those present. For this reason the Church celebrates the baptism of Christ, and calls it "the Feast of Theophany (Immersion)", because He was immersed in the waters of the Jordan. And she also calls it "the Feast of the Divine Manifestation", because He manifested His three hypostases on that day, that is, His essential personal attributes in which the divine Being subsists, and these hypostases are one God.

3.14.2.en: And with this divine manifestation, and the appearance of the Spirit in the form of a dove upon His head, the ministry of Christ on earth begins, just as kings, prophets and priests of old were anointed with oil, which is a sign of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, and then began their ministry; and this is what takes place now in the sacrament of the priesthood in the New Testament.

3.14.3.en: "My beloved Son": He is the Son of God in essence and nature from eternity, which is different from our sonship to God by adoption. "In whom I am well pleased": because He fulfills God's will in the Incarnation, and afterward in redemption for the salvation of mankind.

3.14.4.en: Christ fulfills all righteousness on our behalf in order to teach us to love one another, that we may make up for one another's shortcomings and cover over sins, and so learn humility and service in secret.

3.14.5.en: The temptation on the mountain; the calling of the disciples

4.0.0.en: "Then": that is, after His baptism in the Jordan, He went forward to meet the temptations and overcome them, so that He might give us the power to be victorious. He did not enter into temptation by Himself, in order to teach us not to throw ourselves into it as Lot did by going to Sodom. But if God allows it to us, we strive with His help and overcome it.

4.0.1.en: The Holy Spirit dwelling in Christ led Him into a wilderness near the river Jordan, and He met Satan, because it was familiar in ancient times that demons dwell in the wilds and wastes (deserts), and not in holy places where righteous people are. And He went in order to overcome him, to give us strength and confidence that we will overcome Satan if we fight.

4.0.2.en: And the Lord Christ permitted the devil to tempt Him, to make us feel that He is near to us and feels our temptations, as the Holy Bible says: "For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted" (Heb 2:18), and in order to confirm that temptations must come, so that we may be confident that we shall overcome them, and even receive spiritual blessings from them. But God does not permit him to tempt us except to the extent that benefits us, and He gives us the divine help by which we overcome.

4.1.0.en: In the quiet of solitude, Christ remained forty days in fasting and prayers, to proclaim the importance of being alone with God, even if this is accompanied by the feeling of physical hunger, because being filled with God and enjoying Him is the goal of our life; and this provokes the devil, who dwells in the soul far from God. But when the soul is filled with God, and he tries to fight it, he is defeated.

4.1.1.en: Christ fasted forty days continuously without eating, like Moses and Elijah, so as not to go beyond the limits of human beings, lest people think that He was not an ordinary man, and "afterward he was an hungred" to confirm His humanity. The number 40 is the number 10 multiplied by 4, and the number 10 points to perfection, like the Ten Commandments, and the number 4 points to the four directions of the world; so the number 40 represents the perfection of striving in all directions. Christ accomplished this for our sake, though He had no need of fasting, but as an example for us, to sanctify our fasts.

4.2.0.en: After the devil heard the testimony of heaven about Christ, that He is the Son of God, when He was at the river Jordan, he marveled when he saw Him hungry, and doubted His sonship to God, so he took courage to tempt Him as a man, asking Him to prove His sonship to God by satisfying His hunger by turning the stones into bread. He did not say delicious foods, but merely bread, Satan thereby trying to persuade Him of the necessity of eating lest His body faint. By this temptation he meant to make Him fall into the sin of not relying on God, instead of trusting in His care and that He would provide for Him the food He needed. Christ did not use His divinity for His own comfort; He used it to feed the multitudes (ch. 14:13-21, ch. 15:32-39), to teach us to labor for the comfort of others, and to rely on Him for our needs, confident of His care, fulfilling our duties faithfully.

4.2.1.en: "If thou be the Son of God": a question of doubt, by which he means to make a person doubt himself, and this is the devil's habit in his war with us. It is a provocative question to push us to do what he wants, so that we fall into sin. Therefore we should not hasten to carry out what comes to our mind, for it may be thoughts from the devil, and we should test them by prayer, especially if they concern important decisions, so we take sufficient time for prayer, and we can join it with fasting, that God may guide us and expose the devil's scheme.

4.3.0.en: Christ answered the devil with a verse from the Holy Bible (Deut 8:3), which declares that spiritual satisfaction from the word of God is the foundation, and not only concern for material satisfaction. He did not answer his question about His sonship to God, and declared that the spiritual person is occupied with the word of God before being occupied with his material needs, relying in this on the guidance of the Holy Bible, with which he repels the devil's thoughts.

4.3.1.en: This is the first temptation, and many temptations may have preceded it, but in these three temptations the devil was manifest, for he came forward and confronted Christ; for it is written that he was tempting Him forty days, and not only at their end (Mk 1:13).

4.4.0.en: "Taketh him up": by agreement with Him and not by force, because Christ was willing to be tempted by His own will, to teach us how to overcome the devil.

4.4.1.en: "The holy city": that is, Jerusalem, where the Temple of God is, the holiest place, for the devil fights in every place, even in holy places.

4.4.2.en: "A pinnacle of the temple": a very high place rising above the ground about 200 meters.

4.4.3.en: The second temptation: the devil took Him to the highest place in the Temple, which is its pinnacle, to cast Himself down from above, and the angels would come and bear Him up, and He would descend into the great court carried on their hands, and so would dazzle the gathered crowds, and everyone would know that He is the Son of God, and by this He would begin His ministry.

4.4.4.en: And the devil relied on a verse, to deceive Jesus into thinking that by this He would be fulfilling the word of God, for the divine promise is that He keeps His children by His angels (Ps 91:11-12). It is clear that the devil was still perplexed: is Christ the Son of God, or an ordinary man?!

4.4.5.en: "It is written": the devil resorted to using the word of God in his war, to persuade Christ and make Him fall into temptation, as he does with us, using verses of the Holy Bible and interpreting them according to his wickedness.

4.4.6.en: And the error here is a person's throwing himself into temptation, for God cares for us and rescues us from temptation if it comes upon us, but it is not right for us to throw ourselves into it and then ask God to deliver us.

4.5.0.en: Christ replied to him that God cares for His children, but it is not right for a person to doubt this care and try to test it to make sure of it, nor to throw himself into temptation. But if he falls into temptation, God protects him (Deut 6:16).

4.5.1.en: In this, Christ fled from vainglory, to teach us to work and serve in humility, indeed in secret as far as we are able.

4.6.0.en: The third temptation: the enticement with the glories of the world and its pleasures, and the easy way to reach one's needs, instead of suffering and carrying the cross. So he took Him up into an exceeding high mountain, which points to pride, and there he offered Him the love of possessing the kingdoms of the world, with all the desires and pleasures they carry.

4.6.1.en: "The kingdoms of the world": they are the cities and villages of Judea, which are a sample of the cities of the world with all the glories they carry.

4.7.0.en: The lying devil claimed ownership of all the kingdoms of the world, or perhaps he means his authority over the evil desires with which he entices Jesus, and the condition for obtaining them is submission to him, and the proof of it is worshiping him. The temptation here is the love of possession and leadership, and he offers Christ a solution in place of His coming toil and sufferings, that He would become king over the whole world, and by this free His Jewish people from the Roman occupation, but the condition is submission to the devil and worship of him.

4.8.0.en: "Get thee hence": He clearly declares His rejection of the devil's word and thoughts.

4.8.2.en: "Him only shalt thou serve": He reserves worship for God alone, and therefore forbids offering worship, not only to idols, but every attachment and preoccupation with the desires of the world.

4.8.3.en: Jesus Christ, the second Adam, did not have love of the world in His heart, so He was not affected by the devil's enticements, in addition to His attachment, as man, to the love of God and submission to Him. And He answered him with what is written, that worship is for God alone (Deut 6:13).

4.8.4.en: If the heart submits to God and fears Him, it does not accept the evil desires of the world.

4.9.0.en: Since the devil was defeated by Him, he left Him, but only for a time, to return and fight Him again, as will happen in the attempt of the Pharisees and Sadducees to make Him fall into error. Then the angels came to Him to bear the crowns of His victory up to heaven, for the angels strengthen us and guide us and bear our prayers and our victories up to heaven, that we may be crowned for them in eternity.

4.9.1.en: And Christ faced the temptation alone, so that the victory might be His and not due to the help of the angels.

4.9.2.en: "Leaveth him": this means that every temptation has an end, so that God gives us an opportunity for calm and growth in His love before a second temptation comes, and in this way we are strong before the temptations to come.

4.10.0.en: Christ remained a few months in Judea; John the Evangelist mentioned what happened in it in the first chapters of his Gospel, and during it John the Baptist was completing his preaching and his witness to Christ. Christ stayed this period in Judea to show His agreement in preaching with John the Baptist. During this, many of John's disciples joined Christ. Then after John the Baptist finished his preaching, Herod arrested him and cast him into prison.

4.10.1.en: "Galilee": it is the northern part of Israel, and extends eastward from the river Jordan to Acre in the west on the coast of the Mediterranean.

4.11.0.en: Jesus returned to Galilee, where He had lived in Nazareth in His first years until the age of thirty. But He did not dwell in Nazareth, but went to Capernaum, a well-known city in Galilee, situated on the Sea of Galilee, that is, the Sea of Tiberias, in the places owned by the tribes of Zabulon and Nephthalim (Naphtali).

4.12.0.en: Isaiah prophesied (Isa 9:1-2) about the preaching of Christ in Galilee, and this is the sixth prophecy that St. Matthew mentions about Christ.

4.13.0.en: "The land of Zabulon and the land of Nephthalim": they belong to two tribes of Israel (two sons of Jacob), and lie west of the Jordan and north of the Sea of Galilee.

4.13.1.en: "By the way of the sea": he means the Sea of Galilee.

4.13.2.en: "Beyond Jordan": that is, the land that lies west of the Jordan.

4.13.3.en: "Galilee of the Gentiles": the Jews mixed with the Gentiles in the region of Galilee, therefore it was called "Galilee of the Gentiles", and pagan worship was mixed with Jewish worship, and for this reason the people of Judea despised the inhabitants of this region for their mixing with the worship of the Gentiles. The region of Galilee included the twenty cities that Solomon gave to Hiram because he helped him in building the Temple (1 Kgs 9:11).

4.14.0.en: "The people which sat in darkness": the inhabitants of this land accepted sin and lived in it, which is symbolized by darkness.

4.14.1.en: "Saw great light": light points to the new life with God and to purity, and what is meant here is the proclamation of Christ and His call to them to repent and return to God.

4.14.2.en: "The region and shadow of death" (Ps 107:10): the sins in which the inhabitants of these lands were immersed have death as their punishment. And the word "shadow" means everything connected with death, the evils that lead to it.

4.15.0.en: "From that time": that is, after the arrest of John, Christ began His preaching in Galilee.

4.15.1.en: The preaching of Christ was the same as that which John the Baptist proclaimed, which is quick repentance because of the nearness of the Kingdom of Heaven, that is, the reign of God over hearts, the spiritual reign, which was accomplished by the Resurrection of Christ, and then this Kingdom is completed in the heavens.

4.15.2.en: God seeks you even if you are immersed in sin and mixed with the wicked, and He is ready to purify your heart and renew your life and dwell within you, and even transform you to holiness. So respond to Him by accepting the call to repentance and return to Him, and He will help you and support you and make you prosper in all your steps.

4.16.0.en: "The sea of Galilee": it is a lake with fresh water, 12 miles long and 10 miles wide and about 50 meters deep, and it is the one called the Lake of Tiberias or the Lake of Gennesaret.

4.16.1.en: And as Jesus was walking by the shore of the sea, He found two brothers, Simon, whom He afterward surnamed Peter, that is, Cephas or the Rock, and Andrew his brother, the two sons of Jonas. They were casting their net into the sea, for their trade was catching fish.

4.17.0.en: Christ called them to follow Him and become His disciples, to do a better work, which is catching souls for the knowledge of God, and they obeyed. And this is an extraordinary act, that a person should love God so much that he leaves his necessary work.

4.17.1.en: And obedience is the giving up of human will and reasoning out of love for God. Christ chose His disciples unlettered, and from a region despised in the eyes of the Jews, which is Galilee, to work through them, so that the glory might be to God, and not to human abilities; and the condition for God's work in us is obedience.

4.17.2.en: "Straightway": an indication of quick obedience. It seems that their earlier acquaintance with Christ, mentioned in (Jn 1:40-42), helped them to follow Him, but this shows their being moved and their strong response to the word of God.

4.17.3.en: "They left their nets": the meaning is preferring to follow Christ over their work and their private life, for their love was so strong that they left everything, even the nets and the work by which they lived.

4.18.0.en: "Zebedee": the husband of Salome, who afterward followed Christ (ch. 27:56), and it seems that he was rich and had workers who helped him and had a position in society (Jn 18:15).

4.18.1.en: A little later, as Christ was walking by the shore of the sea, He found two other brothers, James and John the sons of Zebedee, who were partners of Simon and Andrew in catching fish, as their cooperation with them appears in the catching of the great number of fish, after which Jesus called them (Lk 5:6-11); so they left the nets, which they were mending with their father, and followed Jesus.

4.18.2.en: Following God is better than necessary work and the relationship with parents, and this does not mean neglecting our work and not honoring our parents, but that obedience to God is above everything. So be ready to give up some of your comfort and pleasure in order to hold fast to your spiritual life, and then you will enjoy fellowship with God and inner peace.

4.19.0.en: Jesus went out from Capernaum on many journeys in the region of Galilee, about nine journeys, passing through most of its cities and villages, which number more than 200 cities and villages, each of which held on average 15 thousand people, that is, the population of Galilee was about 3 million, and He preached to them repentance and the nearness of the Kingdom.

4.19.1.en: "Their synagogues": places of worship that appeared in the days of the captivity and continued afterward, in which they pray and read the holy Scriptures and deliver spiritual sermons. They were spread throughout the land, because the Temple was only in Jerusalem; and Christ made use of these synagogues in preaching the salvation that He offers to mankind.

4.19.2.en: And Christ was compassionate, healing their diseases to proclaim His love for mankind. Through these miracles hearts were attached to Him, and He spoke to them His deep spiritual words.

4.19.3.en: "All manner of sickness": that is, bodily troubles of which people complained.

4.20.0.en: Because of His miracles and His moving teachings, His fame spread, not only in Galilee, but to many other regions, which are:

4.20.1.en: (1) Syria: a large Roman province lying east of Galilee.

4.20.2.en: (2) Decapolis (the Ten Cities): cities distinguished by Roman privileges, lying east of the Jordan, and now called the Golan. (3) Jerusalem: a well-known city because the Temple of God was in it, lying in the southern part of the land of the Jews. (4) Judea: a region comprising the southern part of the land of the Jews, with the city of Jerusalem inside it, and including many cities and villages.

4.20.3.en: (5) Beyond Jordan: a region lying south of the ten cities.

4.20.4.en: "Those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy": he mentioned these diseases because of their difficulty compared with others. The insane and the epileptics are either afflicted by the works of demons in them, or by nervous diseases that make them unbalanced, or they may sometimes faint and fall to the ground. As for the paralytics, they are those who suffer paralysis in a part or most of their body.

4.20.5.en: May you accustom yourself to do good in every place, helping every needy person and everyone who suffers from weakness, whether he asks you or not; and as they are moved by your love, they readily accept your word about Christ and repentance and returning to God.

4.20.6.en: Chapter 5 The Sermon on the Mount The Beatitudes The completion of the Law
